explain.text:
The selected sentence says the whole adversarial setup is a minimax two-player game, with G and D as opposing players.

In plain terms, a minimax game means one player tries to maximise a shared score while the other tries to minimise it. Here D (the discriminator) tries to maximise the chance of correctly labelling real data and generated samples, while G (the generator) tries to minimise that same score by fooling D. The game is formalised in equation (1), where the value V(D, G) is the expectation of log D(x) over real data plus the expectation of log(1 − D(G(z))) over noise samples z, with G minimising and D maximising. p. 2

The point of calling it a minimax game is that the two models are trained against each other rather than independently. Their competition is what drives G to produce samples that D cannot tell apart from the training data, which is the intended outcome described in the introduction. p. 1

whole.text:
Table 1 reports Parzen window-based log-likelihood estimates for four models (DBN, Stacked CAE, Deep GSN, and adversarial nets) on MNIST and the Toronto Face Database (TFD) p. 6. On MNIST the numbers are the mean log-likelihood of test set samples, with the standard error of the mean computed across examples. On TFD the standard error is computed across folds, with σ cross-validated separately on each fold p. 6. The MNIST comparison uses the real-valued version of the dataset, not the binary one p. 6.

On MNIST, adversarial nets score best at 225 ± 2, ahead of Deep GSN at 214 ± 1.1, DBN at 138 ± 2, and Stacked CAE at 121 ± 1.6 p. 6. On TFD, by contrast, Stacked CAE is highest at 2110 ± 50, with adversarial nets at 2057 ± 26 p. 6.

The authors caution that this likelihood estimation method has fairly high variance and does not perform well in high dimensional spaces, though they call it the best method available to them p. 6.

primer.text:
Before you start
×

The paper proposes training a generator and a discriminator against each other as a minimax game, avoiding Markov chains and approximate inference. It matters because it introduces the adversarial framework, its theory, and its first experiments, which later work builds on.

Key claims

1
A generator G and discriminator D are trained simultaneously; G tries to maximize the chance that D makes a mistake, framed as a minimax game. p. 1
2
For fixed G, the optimal discriminator is D* = p_data / (p_data + p_g). p. 4
3
The global minimum of C(G) is reached if and only if p_g = p_data, with value −log 4, via the Jensen–Shannon divergence. p. 5
4
In practice G is trained to maximize log D(G(z)) instead, because log(1 − D(G(z))) saturates early in learning and gives weak gradients. p. 3
5
Parzen-window log-likelihood estimates put adversarial nets at 225 on MNIST and 2057 on TFD, competitive with the compared models. p. 6

Keep in mind

The theory assumes infinite capacity and an optimal D at each step. The authors concede that real multilayer perceptrons come without such guarantees.
The Parzen window evaluation is described by the authors as high variance and poor in high dimensions, so Table 1 comparisons are weak evidence.
Algorithm 1 as printed uses the minimizing form log(1 − D(G(z))) for G, while the text recommends the maximizing alternative. Also, some text and reference details in this scan look garbled, such as the Table 2 'Helvetica' entry and the missing references 11 to 15.
